editorial_reason: Read Stacks 9.12, Definitions 9.12.2 and 9.12.6 and Lemma 9.12.4. Distinguishes separability of irreducible polynomials, algebraic elements, algebraic field extensions and separable degree.

definitions.text: An irreducible polynomial f∈F[x] is separable if f and its formal derivative f′ are relatively prime; equivalently, f has no repeated root in an algebraic closure of F.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: separable irreducible polynomial

definitions.text: An algebraic element α in a field extension E/F is separable over F if its minimal polynomial over F is separable.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: separable algebraic element

definitions.text: An algebraic extension E/F is separable if every element of E is separable over F.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: separable algebraic extension

definitions.text: The separable degree of an irreducible polynomial f over F is the number of its distinct roots in an algebraic closure of F, counted without multiplicities.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: separable degree of an irreducible polynomial

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 9.6, Definitions 9.6.2 and 9.6.3. It defines both embeddings of fields treated as extensions and chains or towers of successive extensions.

definitions.text: An extension E/F of fields is an inclusion F⊆E of fields; equivalently, it is an injective field homomorphism F→E with the image identified as a subfield of E.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: extension field

definitions.text: A tower of field extensions is a finite sequence of inclusions E_0⊆E_1⊆⋯⊆E_n, so each E_i is a field extension of E_{i−1}.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: tower of extensions

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 5.22, Definition 5.22.1 and Lemma 5.22.2. The inverse-limit definition of a profinite space is equivalent to compact Hausdorff total disconnectedness.

definitions.text: A topological space X is profinite when it is homeomorphic to an inverse limit of finite discrete topological spaces.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: profinite space via finite inverse limits

definitions.text: Equivalently, a topological space is profinite exactly when it is quasi-compact, Hausdorff, and totally disconnected.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: equivalent compact Hausdorff totally disconnected condition

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.67, Definition 10.67.1. Embedded associated primes of a module are nonminimal among its associated primes, and embedded primes of a ring apply this to its regular module.

definitions.text: For an R-module M, an embedded associated prime is a prime p∈Ass_R(M) that is not minimal under inclusion among the associated prime ideals of M.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: embedded associated prime of a module

definitions.text: An embedded prime of a ring R is an embedded associated prime of R considered as an R-module.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: embedded prime ideal of a ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.39, Definitions 4.39.1–4.39.3. This section distinguishes groupoids with trivial automorphism groups from fibred categories with fibres of that kind.

definitions.text: A setoid is a groupoid C in which every object has only its identity automorphism; equivalently, between two objects there is at most one arrow, and its existence is an equivalence relation.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: setoid category

definitions.text: A category fibred in setoids over C is a category fibred in groupoids p:E→C such that each fibre category E_U is a setoid.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: category fibred in setoids

definitions.text: The 2-category fibred in setoids over C has such fibred categories as objects, functors commuting with their projections as 1-morphisms and natural transformations over identity arrows of C as 2-morphisms.
definitions.context_hint: Higher category theory: 2-category of fibred setoids

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.12, Definition 10.12.1 and Lemma 10.12.2. This section gives both bilinear maps and the tensor product's universal characterization, with an explicit quotient construction.

definitions.text: For R-modules M,N,P, a map b:M×N→P is R-bilinear if it is R-linear in M when N is fixed and R-linear in N when M is fixed.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: bilinear map

definitions.text: For R-modules M and N, their tensor product M⊗_R N is an R-module equipped with a bilinear map M×N→M⊗_R N universal among all bilinear maps into R-modules: every bilinear map b:M×N→P factors uniquely through an R-linear map M⊗_R N→P.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: tensor product by universal property

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.92 on countably generated Mittag-Leffler modules, which establishes the projective-module criterion using a countable flat Mittag-Leffler hypothesis. The defining notion of Mittag-Leffler for modules is a tensor-product limit injectivity condition recalled from the preceding section.

definitions.text: An R-module M is Mittag-Leffler if for every family (Q_i) of R-modules, the canonical homomorphism M⊗_R∏_i Q_i→∏_i(M⊗_R Q_i) is injective.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.92 introduction and reference to Section 10.91
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: Mittag-Leffler module via tensor-product comparison

definitions.text: A countably generated R-module M is projective if and only if it is both flat and Mittag-Leffler, in the sense of the canonical tensor-product comparison.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: countably generated projective module criterion

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.109, Definitions 10.109.2 and 10.109.10. Projective dimension pertains to an individual module; global dimension is the uniform supremum of these projective dimensions over all modules.

definitions.text: The projective dimension pd_R(M) of an R-module M is the least integer n≥0 for which there exists an exact projective resolution 0→P_n→⋯→P_0→M→0, or infinity when no finite such resolution exists.
definitions.context_hint: Homological algebra: projective dimension of a module

definitions.text: A ring R has finite global dimension if a finite integer n exists such that every R-module has projective dimension at most n; the minimum such n is the global dimension of R.
definitions.context_hint: Homological algebra: global dimension of a ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.128 'More flatness criteria'. Its lemmas give equivalent local, fibrewise and Tor-based conditions for flatness of modules and finite-type ring maps, all referring to flatness defined elsewhere. This section introduces no standalone new mathematical object corresponding to the section heading, so it is retained as an alternate-formulation lead.

Read Stacks 10.71 Definition 10.71.2 and the paragraph defining Ext via a free resolution and cohomology of the Hom complex. The source defines free resolution and Ext, which should not be merged into one meaning.

definitions.text: A free resolution of an R-module M is an exact augmented chain complex ⋯→F_2→F_1→F_0→M→0 with every F_i a free R-module.
definitions.context_hint: Homological algebra: free resolution

definitions.text: For R-modules M and N, Ext_R^i(M,N) is the ith cohomology of the cochain complex Hom_R(F_•,N) obtained by applying Hom_R(−,N) to a free resolution F_•→M.
definitions.context_hint: Homological algebra: derived Hom or Ext group

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.131, Definitions 10.131.1 and 10.131.2 and Lemma 10.131.3. These distinguish R-derivations from their representing Kähler differential module.

definitions.text: For a ring map R→S and an S-module M, an R-derivation D:S→M is an additive map vanishing on the image of R and satisfying Leibniz's law D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a).
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: derivation relative to a base ring

definitions.text: For a ring map R→S, the module of Kähler differentials Ω_{S/R} is an S-module with a universal R-derivation d:S→Ω_{S/R} such that composition with d gives a bijection Hom_S(Ω_{S/R},M)≅Der_R(S,M) for every S-module M.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Kähler differentials via universal derivation

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 5.17, Definition 5.17.2 and Theorem 5.17.5. It explicitly distinguishes Bourbaki-proper, quasi-proper, universally closed and topologically proper maps and relates the first three.

definitions.text: A continuous map f:X→Y is Bourbaki-proper if the product map id_Z×f:Z×X→Z×Y is closed for every topological space Z.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: Bourbaki-proper map

definitions.text: A continuous map f:X→Y is quasi-proper when the inverse image under f of every quasi-compact subset of Y is quasi-compact in X.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: quasi-proper continuous map

definitions.text: A continuous map f:X→Y is universally closed if every base change f_Z:X×_Y Z→Z along an arbitrary continuous map Z→Y is a closed map.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: universally closed map

definitions.text: A continuous map f:X→Y is proper under the Stacks Project's convention if it is both separated (its diagonal is closed) and universally closed.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: proper map requiring separatedness and universal closedness

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.44 on separable field extensions continued. Its lemmas describe p-bases, separability after changes of ground field and criteria for separably generated extensions, all building on already-defined notions of separability. The chapter heading does not define a new mathematical object.

Read Stacks Categories 4.7 'Examples of fibre products'. This section only demonstrates standard pullback universal properties for special diagrams and categories; it does not introduce a separate concept called an example of a fibre product.

Read Stacks Categories 4.41, the 2-Yoneda lemma. The section proves the 2-categorical analogue of the Yoneda correspondence for categories fibred in groupoids, not a new mathematical definition called '2-Yoneda lemma'.

Read Stacks Commutative Algebra 10.74, 'An application of Ext groups'. The section establishes depth-related consequences of Ext vanishing, using the already-defined Ext functors and module depth; the section contains no independent definition represented by its 'application' heading.
Read Stacks Categories 4.4, Definition 4.4.1. The categorical binary product is specified by the two projection maps and a unique mediator for any cone of arrows.

definitions.text: A product of objects X,Y in a category C is an object P with projections p:P→X and q:P→Y such that for every Z and arrows f:Z→X and g:Z→Y there is a unique arrow h:Z→P with p∘h=f and q∘h=g.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: binary product of objects

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.69, Definition 10.69.1. Quasi-regularity requires the natural graded comparison of polynomial algebra with the associated graded module to be an isomorphism; it is weaker than a regular sequence.

definitions.text: For an R-module M and elements f_1,…,f_c generating J⊆R, the sequence is M-quasi-regular if the graded map (M/JM)⊗_{R/J}(R/J)[X_1,…,X_c]→⊕_{n≥0}J^nM/J^{n+1}M, sending X_i to the class of f_i, is an isomorphism.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: quasi-regular sequence relative to a module

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.105, Definitions 10.105.1 and 10.105.3. These define catenarity of a ring through saturated prime chains and universal catenarity by extension to finite-type algebras.

definitions.text: A commutative ring R is catenary when, for any primes p⊆q, maximal finite chains of primes connecting p to q all have the same length and the possible chain lengths are bounded above.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: catenary ring

definitions.text: A Noetherian ring R is universally catenary if every finitely generated R-algebra is catenary.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: universally catenary Noetherian ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.49, Definition 10.49.1 and Lemmas 10.49.2–10.49.3. The all-base-extensions definition and equivalent integral-over-algebraic-closure criterion should appear as equivalent formulations of one concept.

definitions.text: A k-algebra A is geometrically integral when, for every field extension K/k, the tensor-product algebra A⊗_k K is an integral domain.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: geometrically integral algebra

definitions.text: Equivalently, a k-algebra A is geometrically integral when A⊗_k k̄ is an integral domain, where k̄ is an algebraic closure of k.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: algebraic-closure criterion for geometric integrality
